summary: In this excerpt from Book 11 (part 108), Miranda reports on Hannah's visit to the brick house: she finds Hannah selfish and unwilling to help the younger children or burden Will with poor relations, and Miranda declares Hannah is 'Susan Randall through and through.' Miranda expects the farm mortgage to be cleared by Rebecca or herself rather than Hannah. Rebecca then tells Emma Jane that her piece 'Wareham Wildflowers' has been accepted by The Pilot, to appear in the next issue, while Emma Jane dreams of a shared writing household. The passage closes with Rebecca lamenting the unpaid mortgage and its growing burden.
one_line: Rebecca announces her accepted Pilot piece to Emma Jane, while Miranda judges Hannah selfish and the family mortgage weighs on them.
key_facts: Miranda's impression, conveyed to Jane, was that Hannah was 'close as the bark of a tree' and considerably selfish.
Hannah said she guessed she had done her share already and would not burden Will with her poor relations.
Miranda exclaimed, "She's Susan Randall through and through!"
Miranda said that if the mortgage is ever cleared from the farm, it will be Rebecca or Miranda, not Hannah, who clears it.
Rebecca tells Emma Jane that her contribution entitled 'Wareham Wildflowers' has been accepted for The Pilot.
The senior editor read 'Wareham Wildflowers' and thought it highly instructive; it appears in the next issue of The Pilot.
Emma Jane's poem about the golden gates that close behind us when we leave school was previously published in The Pilot.
Emma Jane says she may not be able to bear the news and asks Rebecca to bury that number of The Pilot with her if anything happens to her.
Rebecca says that whenever she is alone and reads the Pilot back numbers, she almost bursts with pleasure, though her pieces look worse to her each time she reads them.
Emma Jane proposes that when they are older they live together in a little house, where she would do the housework and copying while Rebecca only writes.
Rebecca replies she would like nothing better, but she has promised to keep house for John.
John will not have a house for a good many years, and Rebecca sighs that the mortgage must be paid off first.
The family has not paid the mortgage interest this year, so the day of paying it off grows farther off.
The passage ends with the mortgage itself asking, "Will you pay a little faster?"
